questions.text: 🗣️ (jbtiq_agentic Q38 · S13 Framework Fluency & Cross-Cutting) "Where does LangChain end and LangGraph begin? What's LCEL still for?
points: LCEL/Runnables compose acyclic pipelines — prompt | model | parser — with batteries (streaming, batching, async, retries) for free via the uniform Runnable interface (invoke/stream/batch). Right for chains: RAG pipelines, extraction, anything without cycles.

LangGraph exists because agents are loops: cycles, branching on state, persistence — things a pipe syntax can't express. Graph over typed state with checkpointing is the agent runtime; LCEL components typically live inside graph nodes.

The boundary rule: no cycles and no persistent state → LCEL; loops, interrupts, or durable state → LangGraph. Modern LangChain agent abstractions are built on LangGraph underneath — worth saying to show currency.

Supporting cast fluency: structured output parsers, document loaders/splitters, retriever abstractions — commodity plumbing; the differentiated layers are the graph design and your tools/evals, consistent with the framework-vs-no-framework judgment earlier.

questions.text: 🗣️ (jbtiq_agentic Q39 · S13 Framework Fluency & Cross-Cutting) "Structured output: how do you actually guarantee the model returns valid JSON matching your schema — and what can still go wrong?
points: The ladder: prompt-and-pray → function-calling/JSON mode (provider-enforced JSON) → constrained/grammar-based decoding (invalid tokens masked at generation — schema validity guaranteed by construction) → parse-validate-repair loops (Pydantic validation, feed errors back for one retry) as the pragmatic wrapper at any rung.

Know the mechanism difference: JSON mode guarantees syntactic JSON, not your schema; schema-constrained decoding (structured outputs) guarantees the shape too. Say which your provider actually gives you.

What still goes wrong: semantically wrong but valid values (the real residual risk — the enum is legal, the choice is wrong), over-constrained schemas degrading content quality (the model contorts to satisfy shape), required fields the model can't know (it will fabricate rather than omit — make them optional with explicit "unknown").

Production stance: schema validation is the floor (never parse raw text downstream); business-rule validation on top; and log validation-failure rates per schema — a rising rate flags prompt/model drift before users see it.
This is the backbone of agent reliability: every tool argument is structured output — the same ladder applies at every step of the loop.
questions.badge: Trending — structured-output reliability recurs on LeetCode Discuss + production posts (2025–26)
questions.oneLiner: Climb the ladder from JSON mode to schema-constrained decoding so shape is guaranteed by construction, wrap with validate-and-repair — and remember valid isn't true: semantic wrongness inside a legal schema is the residual risk, so business rules and failure-rate monitoring sit on top.

questions.text: 🗣️ (jbtiq_agentic Q41 · S13 Framework Fluency & Cross-Cutting) "Define autonomy levels for agents the way you'd present them to a risk committee.
points: A workable ladder: L0 suggest (human executes everything — copilot), L1 act-with-approval (agent prepares, human approves each consequential action), L2 act-with-oversight (agent executes within scoped permissions, humans review samples/exceptions), L3 delegated (agent owns the task end-to-end within budgets, humans set policy and audit). Frame each rung by what the human stops doing.

The committee's variables per rung: blast radius (what the agent can touch), reversibility of its actions, detection (how fast a bad action surfaces), and accountability (who answers for an agent action — the deploying team, with the audit trail as evidence).

The key governance move: autonomy is granted per action class, not per agent — one agent can be L3 on reads, L1 on refunds; and it's earned empirically — promotion to a higher rung requires demonstrated success rates and incident-free volume at the current one.
Include demotion: incident triggers, drift alarms, or eval regressions drop the autonomy level automatically — a ratchet that only tightens upward is how trust survives the first incident.
This maps directly onto the permission/HITL architecture — autonomy levels are the policy layer those mechanisms enforce.
questions.badge: Evergreen (the governance-fluency question)
questions.oneLiner: Suggest, approve-each, oversee-by-sampling, delegate-within-budgets — granted per action class, earned by demonstrated success at the previous rung, and automatically demotable on incidents, with blast radius, reversibility and auditability as the committee's variables.

questions.text: 🗣️ (jbtiq_agentic Q43 · S13 Framework Fluency & Cross-Cutting) "Two of your agents keep undoing each other's work on shared records. Diagnose the coordination problem class and fix it.
points: Name it: a write-write conflict from unsynchronized concurrent actors — lost updates, races, and livelock (each agent "correcting" the other) — the classic distributed-systems problem wearing an agent costume. LLMs add a twist: agents re-derive intent from stale reads, so they conflict semantically, not just at the row level.

Mechanisms that transfer unchanged: ownership partitioning (one writer per record class/region — the best fix is making the conflict impossible), optimistic concurrency (version numbers on records; a stale write fails and the agent re-reads before retrying), and leases/locks for genuinely shared critical sections.

Agent-specific additions: put shared intent in explicit shared state (a task board both read before acting) instead of each inferring it; and give the orchestrator the arbitration role — peer agents negotiating writes via natural language is how you get livelock with token bills.
Detection: audit trails per record show interleaved agent writes — instrument write provenance (which agent, which run) or you'll debug this blind.
The framing line: multi-agent coordination is distributed systems plus semantic drift — solve the classical layer with classical tools, then remove ambiguity about who owns what.
questions.badge: Evergreen (distributed-systems-in-agent-clothing)
questions.oneLiner: It's a lost-update race between unsynchronized writers — partition ownership so the conflict can't happen, back it with optimistic versioning and leases, and move shared intent into explicit state, because agents negotiating writes conversationally is livelock with a token bill.

questions.text: 🗣️ (jbtiq_agentic Q44 · S13 Framework Fluency & Cross-Cutting) "CoT, ToT, GoT — the reasoning-structure zoo. What survives contact with production, and what did reasoning models change?
points: The ideas: CoT — decompose before answering; ToT — explore multiple branches with lookahead and backtracking, needs an evaluator to score branches; GoT — arbitrary merge/refine topologies over thoughts. Each trades tokens for solution quality on search-shaped problems.

What survived production: CoT is now table stakes (and increasingly internalized); branch-and-evaluate survives as best-of-N with a verifier/reranker — the pragmatic ToT — for problems with checkable answers. Full ToT/GoT scaffolds mostly stayed papers: cost explodes and the branch evaluator is the weak link.

What reasoning models changed: extended internal deliberation moved much of the explicit scaffolding into the model (train-time and inference-time compute scaling); you now buy reasoning depth as a model parameter rather than orchestrating it — prompt-level thought-structuring earns less than it did.

The durable architecture lesson: external structure still wins where you have a strong external verifier (tests, math checkers, simulators) — sample diverse candidates, verify, select; that's search with the model as proposal distribution.
Interview positioning: show you know the papers, then show you know that in production the question is "where's my verifier and what's my token budget", not which acronym.
questions.badge: Trending — "is ToT real or a paper?" recurs on LeetCode Discuss + practitioner posts (2025–26)
questions.oneLiner: CoT became table stakes and largely moved inside reasoning models; ToT survives as best-of-N against a real verifier; the full tree and graph scaffolds mostly stayed papers — external reasoning structure earns its tokens only where an external verifier can score branches.

questions.text: 🗣️ (jbtiq_agentic Q45 · S13 Framework Fluency & Cross-Cutting) "Close it out: how do you, as the architect, frame agentic AI to a skeptical CTO — what's real, what's hype, what do you commit to?
points: What's real today: agents work where outcomes are verifiable, actions are reversible or gated, and value-per-task funds the loop — coding, research synthesis, tiered support, data analysis with semantic layers. The wins are workflow-adjacent, not AGI-adjacent.

What's structurally unsolved: compounding reliability over long trajectories, prompt injection (no in-band fix), and evaluation of open-ended work — these are managed with architecture, not eliminated; anyone selling "fully autonomous everything" is selling past the reliability math.

The commit-either-way investments: tool contracts over systems of record, eval sets and trace pipelines, permissioning/audit — they pay off under any model trajectory and compound as models improve ("build the harness; the engine keeps upgrading").

The strategy: ladder of autonomy earned per use case with SLOs and demotion triggers; start where errors are cheap and verification is cheap; measure cost-per-task against the human baseline honestly, including the failure and review overhead.

End on the asymmetry: model capability is the fastest-improving input in the stack — architect so that a better model drops in and everything gets better, which means owning the boring layers and renting the intelligence.
questions.badge: Trending — the synthesis question senior loops end on (2025–26)
questions.oneLiner: Agents are real where verification is cheap and errors are gated, structurally hard on long-trajectory reliability and injection — so we invest in the harness that pays under any model future: tools, evals, traces and permissions, with autonomy earned per use case against SLOs.
